title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: After his talk with Pierre in Moscow, Prince Andrew went to Petersburg — on business, he told his family, but really to meet Anatole Kuragin, whom he felt he had to confront. On reaching Petersburg he asked for Kuragin, but Kuragin had already left the city. Pierre had warned his brother-in-law that Prince Andrew was on his track. Anatole Kuragin promptly got an appointment from the Minister of War and went to join the army in Moldavia. While in Petersburg, Prince Andrew met Kutuzov, his former commander, who had always been well disposed toward him. Kutuzov suggested that he come along to the army in Moldavia, where the old general had just been appointed commander in chief. So Prince Andrew received a post on the headquarters staff and left for Turkey.

Prince Andrew did not think it proper to write and challenge Kuragin. He reasoned that challenging him without some fresh cause might compromise the young Countess Rostova, so he wanted to meet Kuragin in person and find a new pretext for a duel. But in Turkey too he failed to meet him, because Kuragin returned to Russia soon after Prince Andrew arrived. In a new country, amid new conditions, Prince Andrew found life easier to bear. His betrothed had broken faith with him, and the harder he tried to hide the effects, the more sharply he felt them. The surroundings where he had once been happy became painful to him, and the freedom and independence he had once prized so highly were more painful still. He could no longer think the thoughts that had first come to him as he lay gazing at the sky on the field of Austerlitz, that he had later developed with Pierre, and that had filled his solitude at Bogucharovo and then in Switzerland and Rome. He even dreaded to recall them, and the bright, boundless horizons they had opened. Now he cared only about the nearest practical matters, which had nothing to do with his past interests, and the more those past interests were closed to him, the more eagerly he seized on these. It was as if the lofty, infinite canopy of heaven that had once towered above him had suddenly turned into a low, solid vault that weighed him down — a place where everything was clear, but nothing was eternal or mysterious.

Of the activities open to him, army service was the simplest and most familiar. As a general on duty on Kutuzov's staff, he threw himself into the work with zeal and perseverance, and he surprised Kutuzov by how willing and exact he was. He had not found Kuragin in Turkey, and he did not think it necessary to rush back to Russia after him. All the same, he knew that however long it might be before they met, he would not be able to resist calling Kuragin out when they did — any more than a starving man can help snatching at food. This held despite his contempt for Kuragin and despite all the proofs he found to convince himself that stooping to a quarrel with him was not worth it. And the awareness that the insult was not yet avenged, that his rancor was still unspent, weighed on his heart. It poisoned the artificial tranquillity he managed to win in Turkey through restless, plodding, rather vainglorious and ambitious activity.

In the year 1812, news of the war with Napoleon reached Bucharest, where Kutuzov had been living for two months, spending his days and nights with a Wallachian woman. Prince Andrew asked Kutuzov to transfer him to the Western Army. Kutuzov was already weary of Bolkonski's activity, which seemed a reproach to his own idleness, and he let him go very readily, giving him a mission to Barclay de Tolly.

Before joining the Western Army, which was then, in May, encamped at Drissa, Prince Andrew visited Bald Hills. It lay directly on his way, only two miles off the Smolensk highroad. In the last three years there had been so many changes in his life, and he had thought, felt and seen so much (he had traveled in both the east and the west), that on reaching Bald Hills he found it strange and unexpected that the way of life there was unchanged, the same in every detail. He passed through the gates with their stone pillars and drove up the avenue to the house as if entering an enchanted, sleeping castle. The same old stateliness, the same cleanliness, the same stillness reigned there. Inside were the same furniture, the same walls, sounds and smell, and the same timid faces, only somewhat older. Princess Mary was still the same timid, plain maiden getting on in years, uselessly and joylessly spending the best years of her life in fear and constant suffering. Mademoiselle Bourienne was the same coquettish, self-satisfied girl, enjoying every moment of her existence and full of joyful hopes for the future. She had merely become more self-confident, Prince Andrew thought. Dessalles, the tutor he had brought from Switzerland, wore a coat of Russian cut and spoke broken Russian to the servants, but he was still the same narrowly intelligent, conscientious and pedantic teacher. The old prince had changed in appearance only by the loss of a tooth, which left a noticeable gap on one side of his mouth. In character he was the same as ever, only more irritable and more skeptical about what was happening in the world. Little Nicholas alone had changed. He had grown, filled out and turned rosy, and he had curly dark hair. When he was merry and laughing, he lifted the upper lip of his pretty little mouth quite unconsciously, just as the little princess used to do. He alone did not obey the law of immutability in the enchanted, sleeping castle. But though everything looked as it always had, the inner relations among these people had changed since Prince Andrew last saw them. The household was divided into two alien and hostile camps, who changed their habits for his sake and met only because he was there. To one camp belonged the old prince, Mademoiselle Bourienne and the architect; to the other, Princess Mary, Dessalles, little Nicholas and all the old nurses and maids.

While Prince Andrew stayed at Bald Hills, the whole family dined together, but they were ill at ease. He felt like a visitor for whose sake an exception was being made, and that his presence made everyone awkward. He felt this despite himself at dinner on the first day and kept silent. The old prince noticed it and also became morosely quiet, and he retired to his rooms right after dinner. In the evening Prince Andrew went to him and, trying to draw him out, began to tell him about the young Count Kamensky's campaign. Unexpectedly the old prince began to talk about Princess Mary. He blamed her for her superstitions and for her dislike of Mademoiselle Bourienne, who, he said, was the only person truly attached to him.

The old prince said that if he was ill, it was only because of Princess Mary: she deliberately worried and irritated him, and with her indulgence and silly talk she was spoiling little Prince Nicholas. The old prince knew very well that he tormented his daughter and that her life was very hard, but he also knew that he could not help tormenting her and that she deserved it. "Why doesn't Prince Andrew, who sees this, say anything to me about his sister? Does he take me for a scoundrel, or for an old fool who keeps his own daughter at a distance for no reason and attaches this Frenchwoman to himself? He doesn't understand, so I must explain it, and he must hear me out," thought the old prince. And he began explaining why he could not put up with his daughter's unreasonable character.

"Since you ask me," said Prince Andrew, without looking up (he was criticizing his father for the first time in his life), "I did not want to speak about it, but as you ask, I will give you my frank opinion. If there is any misunderstanding and discord between you and Mary, I can't blame her for it at all. I know how she loves and respects you. Since you ask me," Prince Andrew went on, growing irritable, as he had been liable to do lately, "I can only say that if there are any misunderstandings, they are caused by that worthless woman, who is not fit to be my sister's companion."
At first the old man stared fixedly at his son. An unnatural smile showed the fresh gap between his teeth, which Prince Andrew could not get used to.
"What companion, my dear boy? Eh? You've already been talking it over! Eh?"

"Father, I did not want to judge," said Prince Andrew in a hard, bitter tone, "but you challenged me, and I have said, and always will say, that Mary is not to blame. Those to blame — the one to blame — is that Frenchwoman."

"Ah, he has passed judgment... passed judgment!" said the old man in a low voice and, as it seemed to Prince Andrew, with some embarrassment. But then he suddenly jumped up and cried: "Be off, be off! Let not a trace of you remain here!..."

Prince Andrew wanted to leave at once, but Princess Mary persuaded him to stay another day. That day he did not see his father, who stayed in his room and admitted no one but Mademoiselle Bourienne and Tikhon, though he asked several times whether his son had gone. Next day, before leaving, Prince Andrew went to his son's rooms. The boy, curly-headed like his mother and glowing with health, sat on his knee, and Prince Andrew began telling him the story of Bluebeard, but fell into a reverie before he finished it. He was not thinking about this pretty child, his son, whom he held on his knee, but about himself. He searched himself for either remorse at having angered his father or regret at leaving home for the first time in his life on bad terms with him, and was horrified to find neither. It meant still more to him that he searched for the old tenderness for his son and did not find it, though he had hoped to reawaken it by caressing the boy and taking him on his knee.
"Well, go on!" said his son.
Prince Andrew, without replying, put him down from his knee and went out of the room.

As soon as Prince Andrew gave up his daily occupations, and especially once he was back in the old conditions of life where he had been happy, weariness of life overcame him with its former intensity. He hurried to escape from these memories and to find some work as soon as possible.
"So you've decided to go, Andrew?" asked his sister.
"Thank God that I can," replied Prince Andrew. "I am very sorry you can't."
"Why do you say that?" replied Princess Mary. "Why do you say that, when you are going off to this terrible war, and he is so old? Mademoiselle Bourienne says he has been asking about you...."
As soon as she began to speak of it, her lips trembled and her tears began to fall. Prince Andrew turned away and began pacing the room.
"Ah, my God! my God! When one thinks who and what — what trash — can cause people misery!" he said, with a malignity that alarmed Princess Mary.
She understood that by "trash" he meant not only Mademoiselle Bourienne, the cause of her misery, but also the man who had ruined his own happiness.

"Andrew! There is one thing I beg, I entreat of you!" she said, touching his elbow and looking at him with eyes that shone through her tears. "I understand you" (she looked down). "Don't imagine that sorrow is the work of men. Men are His tools." She looked a little above Prince Andrew's head, with the confident, habitual look with which one looks at the place where a familiar portrait hangs. "Sorrow is sent by Him, not by men. Men are His instruments; they are not to blame. If you think someone has wronged you, forget it and forgive! We have no right to punish. And then you will know the happiness of forgiving."

"If I were a woman I would do so, Mary. That is a woman's virtue. But a man should not and cannot forgive and forget," he replied. Until that moment he had not been thinking of Kuragin, but now all his unspent anger suddenly swelled up in his heart.

"If Mary is already urging me to forgive, it means I ought to have punished him long ago," he thought. And without answering her further, he began to think of the glad, vindictive moment when he would meet Kuragin, who he knew was now in the army.

Princess Mary begged him to stay one day more. She said she knew how unhappy her father would be if Andrew left without being reconciled to him. But Prince Andrew replied that he would probably be back from the army soon and would certainly write to his father, and that the longer he stayed now, the more bitter their differences would become.
"Good-by, Andrew! Remember that misfortunes come from God, and men are never to blame," were the last words he heard from his sister as he took leave of her.

"Then it must be so!" thought Prince Andrew as he drove out of the avenue from the house at Bald Hills. "She, poor innocent creature, is left to be victimized by an old man who has outlived his wits. The old man feels he is guilty but cannot change himself. My boy is growing up and rejoicing in life, in which, like everybody else, he will deceive or be deceived. And I am off to the army. Why? I don't know myself. I want to meet that man whom I despise, to give him a chance to kill me and laugh at me!"

These conditions of life had been the same before, but then they had all been connected; now they had all tumbled to pieces. Only senseless things, lacking coherence, presented themselves one after another to Prince Andrew's mind.
